title: Walmart just took another step to beat Costco that could backfire
detail:
Walmart just took another step to beat Costco that could backfire
Maurie Backman
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 6:33 AM PST 4 min read
WMT
COST
ZIPL.PVT
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Walmart and Costco are natural competitors. Both retailers have built their businesses around offering shoppers competitive prices, a wide selection of merchandise, and opportunities to save money.

But while the two companies share many similarities, they have different ideas about what keeps customers coming back.

Walmart has increasingly focused on making shopping more convenient, particularly through its growing delivery business. 

Costco, meanwhile, continues to emphasize its in-store experience, giving members reasons to visit and discover products they might not have planned to purchase.

Now, Walmart is making another major investment in convenience that could give it an advantage over its warehouse rival.

Walmart sees delivery as a competitive advantage

On Nov. 5, Walmart announced a new multi-year agreement with drone delivery company Zipline to add 300 drone delivery locations across the United States, expanding a program that has already completed more than 2 million deliveries.

The move gives Walmart another way to attract shoppers who want everyday essentials delivered quickly without making a trip to a store. And that could become an increasingly important competitive advantage as consumers prioritize convenience alongside affordability.

Read more: Costco and Walmart offer very different Thanksgiving meal costs

Walmart's expanded partnership with Zipline will make drone delivery available to more customers nationwide, with tens of thousands of eligible items available for delivery in as fast as 30 minutes in areas where the service operates.

Customers can select drone delivery through Walmart's website or app if their addresses fall within an eligible delivery area. 

Zipline CEO and co-founder Keller Cliffton highlighted how consumer behavior has changed since the partnership began.

"Five years ago, Walmart and Zipline made our first deliveries together," said Cliffton. "Today, customers order from us multiple times a day. When you can get what you need in 10-30 minutes it takes a huge amount of anxiety out of life. People can plan their lives around their loved ones, not errands."

Walmart also offers several other delivery options, including delivery in 30 minutes or less in select markets and one-hour express delivery.

Expanding those options gives shoppers more reasons to use Walmart for everyday purchases rather than turning to competitors or third-party delivery services. It also creates opportunities for Walmart to increase shopping frequency and build customer loyalty.

title: Warren Buffett Said This 1 Mistake Cost Berkshire About $10 Billion. Here’s How Investors Can Avoid It.
detail:
Warren Buffett Said This 1 Mistake Cost Berkshire About $10 Billion. Here’s How Investors Can Avoid It.
Matt DiLallo, The Motley Fool
Sat, November 14, 2026 at 7:25 AM PST 5 min read
BRK-B
WMT
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

Warren Buffett never hid from his investment mistakes. Instead, he wanted to learn from them. One of his most expensive blunders wasn't a bad purchase, but one he never completed.

At Berkshire Hathaway's (NYSE:BRKA)(NYSE:BRKB) 2004 annual meeting, Buffett confessed that his worst mistake was Walmart (NASDAQ:WMT). While he initially wanted to buy 100 million shares of the retail giant, Berkshire bought only a small amount because, as the price went up, Buffett waited for it to come back down, which never happened. His reluctance to pay a little more turned out to be a $10 billion mistake.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

The mistake wasn't buying a bad stock. It was getting too anchored to a price on a good one. That's a trap almost every investor falls into, and it's easy to avoid once you know what to look for.

Image source: Getty Images.

What actually went wrong

Walmart was exactly the kind of business Buffett wanted to own. It was a dominant low-cost leader. He set his sights on buying 100 million shares at a pre-split price of $23. Buffett bought some shares, but then the price rose slightly. He thought it might come back down, so he waited. That pullback never came. In hindsight, he said paying a little more would have been inconsequential compared to the gains the stock would go on to deliver.

Buffett did try to fix this mistake. Berkshire built a new Walmart stake starting in 2005, which was worth nearly $6 billion by 2016, the year it sold most of it.

The math of waiting

Berkshire's missed gains on Walmart show why anchoring can be so costly. If you think a $50 stock has the potential to gain 50% over the next few years, paying 5% more ($52.50) than your desired price would yield a 43% return. That's not a bad return. Waiting for the price to come back down to your target, on the other hand, risks the entire upside if it never does. A small premium costs you a little in the long run, while a missed position costs you the whole gain.

3 ways to avoid the same mistake

Decide what it's worth before you look at the price. Calculate the estimated future value for a stock you'd be happy to own before you start buying. The target price then becomes a comparison point rather than an anchor.

Set your purchases in advance. Consider splitting the position into thirds: buy one third now, another on a pullback, and the final third on a date you pick regardless of price. That way you won't freeze in the face of a rising price like Buffett.

Compare the extra cost to the upside you expect. Before you pass on a stock because it has risen, run the math. If you expected it to gain 50% from your target price and it now costs 5% more than when you first looked, you would still earn about 43% on this purchase. If that's not a worthwhile return, you might not have as much conviction in the stock as you think.

Walmart recently agreed to a record US$7.8 million settlement with Pennsylvania authorities over Child Labor Act violations and is rolling out new energy, AI shopping, and drone delivery initiatives while preparing to report third quarter earnings on 19 November 2026.

A stronger focus on omnichannel services, advertising, membership programs, and partnerships such as Base Power is reshaping how Walmart earns beyond traditional in-store retailing.

This article examines how Walmart's expanding digital and services strategy, including new AI tools, fits into the existing investment narrative.

Spot 31 resilient stocks with low risk scores that, like Walmart, pair scaled operations and a strong compliance focus with resilience that can matter when regulatory headlines hit the front page.

Walmart Investment Narrative Recap

To own Walmart, you need to believe its omnichannel machine, membership, marketplace and advertising efforts can keep comp growth and profit expanding even while core U.S. retailing faces cost pressure. The big near term driver is the 19 November earnings update, where investors want clarity on pricing investments, tariff refund reinvestment and holiday demand.

The Pennsylvania child labor settlement looks manageable in dollar terms for a business with more than US$735.8b of revenue, but it does highlight compliance as a real operating risk. The bigger near term swing factor is whether price cuts and e commerce mix weigh on margins more than expected.

The Pennsylvania enforcement action makes Walmart's broader compliance posture more relevant. Recent steps such as expanding the Third Party Laboratory Assignment List to include SGS signal the retailer is tightening product testing and quality controls across apparel, especially for children and baby categories where safety scrutiny is intense.

That move can support the omnichannel and digital services push that prakhar_ef9px, a Simply Wall St Community investor who wrote the Narrative, sees as a key growth engine in Walmart's "Other" SBU. Stronger lab oversight may limit disruption and reputational setbacks, which matters if advertising, marketplace and new service lines are going to carry more of the growth burden.

Using revenue growth of 13.0% a year and a future profit margin of 3.1% for Walmart, the valuation narrative from prakhar_ef9px arrives at a fair value estimate of US$154.58 per share, tying that number directly to the expected scale and profitability of the "Other" SBU over time.

Walmart WMT shares have seen a modest bid in recent weeks, likely reflecting the company's defensive attributes as the more glamorous AI trade has lost some of its earlier luster. Despite recent struggles, Walmart shares outperformed peers like Target TGT and even Amazon AMZN over the last five years, up more than +175% vs. +49.7% for Amazon and -27.8% for Target. Walmart's +175% gain over the last five years compares to a +79% gain for the S&P 500 index.

Unlike this standout performance over the last five years, Walmart shares seem to have lost their mojo this year, even though they seem to be rebounding lately, as the year-to-date performance chart below for Walmart, Target, Amazon, and the S&P 500 index shows.

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Walmart shares were down sharply after the last quarterly release on August 20th, reflecting a combination of factors, including a seemingly lower-quality earnings beat (benefiting from tariff refunds), decelerating comp growth, and underwhelming Q3 guidance.

It will be interesting to see whether Thursday, November 19th's quarterly release helps the stock build on its recovery. We should keep in mind that we will have seen results from Target ahead of Walmart's release, with Target reporting results before the market's open on Wednesday, November 18th. As we saw in the performance chart above, Target shares have been enjoying a strong market run, outperforming Walmart and the broader market by a mile.

Walmart and other big-box retailers are undoubtedly facing a difficult operating environment, with elevated fuel costs adding to consumers' financial burdens and increasing retailers' expenses. These macro overhangs partly accounted for management's softish guidance for Q3.

It is important to keep in mind that Walmart shares command a premium valuation, trading currently at 40.1X forward 12-month EPS estimates, only modestly below the 10-year high valuation multiple of 45.4X in February 2026. This represents a significant expansion in the valuation premium relative to Target, as the chart below of the two stocks' 10-year valuation history shows

Zacks Investment Research

Image Source: Zacks Investment Research

Market participants expect stocks commanding premium valuation multiples to beat-and-raise when they report results, which is not what we saw from Walmart.

Despite the negative effects of elevated fuel costs on consumer spending and the company's freight costs, Walmart remains better positioned than many others in the space given its value orientation, greater indexing to groceries, and robust digital capabilities. Walmart has been consistently gaining market share among higher-income households in recent years, which has more than offset affordability-based demand softness from its lower-income consumers.

For the full year, the Zacks Consensus Estimates project earnings of $2.88 per share and a revenue of $751.49 billion, demonstrating changes of +9.09% and +5.37%, respectively, from the preceding year.

Additionally, investors should keep an eye on any recent revisions to analyst forecasts for Walmart. Such recent modifications usually signify the changing landscape of near-term business trends. Therefore, positive revisions in estimates convey analysts' confidence in the business performance and profit potential.

Our research reveals that these estimate alterations are directly linked with the stock price performance in the near future. To utilize this, we have created the Zacks Rank, a proprietary model that integrates these estimate changes and provides a functional rating system.

The Zacks Rank system, which varies between #1 (Strong Buy) and #5 (Strong Sell), carries an impressive track record of exceeding expectations, confirmed by external audits, with stocks at #1 delivering an average annual return of +25% since 1988. Valuation is also important, so investors should note that Walmart has a Forward P/E ratio of 43.89 right now. This valuation marks a premium compared to its industry average Forward P/E of 13.98.

It's also important to note that WMT currently trades at a PEG ratio of 4.57. The PEG ratio is akin to the commonly utilized P/E ratio, but this measure also incorporates the company's anticipated earnings growth rate. Everyone knows Walmart (NASDAQ: WMT). It's a retail behemoth, with a recent market value of roughly $1 trillion and some 10,900 stores in 19 countries. It employs about 2.1 million people worldwide and serves some 280 million customers. (With Earth's population of 8 billion people, there's clearly room for growth for Walmart, despite its large size.) Indeed, Walmart is one of Earth's largest employers.

Image source: The Motley Fool.

Clearly, the company has been doing well in recent years. (The stock gained 73.5% in 2024 alone!) But all that growth has left the stock rather overvalued, with a recent price-to-sales ratio of 1.37, well above the five-year average of 0.85, and a recent forward-looking price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio of 38, well above the five-year average of 27.

Should you invest in Walmart?

So, should you invest in Walmart? I would hold off, as you'd be paying a steep per-share price. The stock will likely continue to grow over the coming decades, but it may also retreat to a more reasonable valuation in the next year or two -- especially if there's a stock market crash.

Think of it this way: The stock was recently priced around $126 per share. If you buy now and it hits $200 in five years, you'll enjoy a roughly 60% gain -- about 10% annually on average. But if you choose to wait, hoping for a better price, and you can snag shares at, say, $100 per share, you'll enjoy a 100% gain when the shares hit $200 (about 15% annualized).

Buying some shares now could serve you well, as long as you're planning to hold for many years. But there are other, less richly valued portfolio candidates out there, too.
